plan: Humanities passage (CLD-P-ACT-R-000068), an original essay on John Cage's 4′33″: David Tudor's 1952 premiere near Woodstock, Cage's claim that the piece frames ambient sound, his anechoic-chamber experience at Harvard, critics' competing views, and the author's view that its achievement is a change in attention. Topic checked against every bank (no matches). Nine new questions, three aimed at hard. Plus R067-03 resubmitted as revision 2 on banked passage CLD-P-ACT-R-000067. Difficulty provisional.

passages.title: Four Minutes of Listening
passages.text:
On an August evening in 1952, in a concert hall near Woodstock, New York, the pianist David Tudor sat down at a piano, closed the lid over the keys, and started a stopwatch. For the next four minutes and thirty-three seconds, divided into three movements that he marked by opening and closing the lid, he played nothing. The piece was John Cage's 4′33″, and many in the audience left convinced that they had been the victims of a joke.

Cage insisted that they had not been. The piece, he argued, was not silent at all. During the first movement, listeners could hear the wind outside; during the second, raindrops on the roof; during the third, the audience itself, talking and walking out. The performer's silence was meant to frame these sounds, which were always present but which concertgoers had been trained to ignore.

Cage had come to this view partly through an experience not long before. He visited an anechoic chamber at Harvard University, a room built to absorb sound so completely that nothing echoes. Expecting perfect silence, he instead heard two sounds, one high and one low. An engineer told him that these were his own nervous system and his own blood in circulation. Cage concluded that true silence does not exist for a living listener; there is only sound we attend to and sound we do not.

Critics have never fully agreed about what to make of the result. For some, 4′33″ is a philosophical statement more than a musical work, an idea that loses its force once it has been understood. For others, it is a genuine composition that changes with every performance, since no two rooms and no two audiences sound the same.

Both views, perhaps, miss the piece's quietest achievement. Whatever 4′33″ is, it is difficult to hear it once without listening differently afterward. A listener who has sat through it may find, walking out of the hall, that the traffic and voices of the street have become something worth noticing. That change in attention, more than any argument about whether the piece counts as music, may be what Cage was after.

passages.title: The Feeling of Knowing
passages.text:
In the 1880s, the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus became his own experimental subject. He memorized long lists of nonsense syllables, such as "dax" and "bok," chosen so that no meaning or association could help him, and then tested himself after intervals ranging from minutes to a month. Most of what he learned slipped away within the first day, and the loss then slowed. He also found that lists he relearned on several separate days stayed with him far longer than lists he crammed in a single sitting.

A century later, researchers began asking a related question: what kind of studying best slows forgetting? In one well-known experiment, students read a short passage and then either read it again or tried to write down as much of it as they could remember, with no feedback. Five minutes later, the students who had reread the passage remembered slightly more. A week later, the pattern had reversed: the students who had practiced recalling the passage remembered far more than those who had reread it.

The most striking result, however, concerned the students' own predictions. Asked how well they expected to remember the passage, the rereaders were more confident than the students who had practiced recall. Rereading had made the material feel familiar, and the students mistook that familiarity for learning.

Psychologists now describe this mistake as an illusion of fluency. Material that has just been reread is processed easily, and that ease feels like mastery. Trying to recall material, by contrast, is effortful and often frustrating; a student who struggles to remember a passage may conclude that the method is not working, even as the struggle is strengthening the memory.

None of this means that rereading is useless or that every struggle is productive. Effort that leads nowhere, such as attempting a test on material one has never seen, does little good. But the research suggests that the comfort many students seek in their study habits may be a poor guide to what those habits accomplish. The methods that feel least effective in the moment are sometimes the ones that last.

candidates.stem: The main idea of the passage is that John Cage's 4′33″:

choices.A: was a joke that Cage later admitted had confused his audience.
choices.B: proves that a composition must contain musical notes to count as music.
choices.C: was meant to redirect listeners' attention to sounds they usually ignore.
choices.D: was the first piece of music ever performed without a piano being played.

candidates.evidence: That change in attention, more than any argument about whether the piece counts as music, may be what Cage was after
candidates.explanation: The passage explains that Cage meant the silence to frame ambient sounds and concludes that the piece's aim was to change how listeners pay attention.

A.rationale: Cage insisted it was not a joke.

B.rationale: The passage does not argue this, and critics are said to disagree.

D.rationale: The passage makes no claim about being the first such piece.

hints: What does the last paragraph suggest Cage wanted?
candidates.remember: A main-idea answer must include the passage's conclusion.

author_checklist.hardness: the conclusion reframes the earlier debate

candidates.stem: According to the passage, during the performance David Tudor marked the three movements by:

choices.A: opening and closing the lid over the keys.
choices.B: playing a single note at the start of each one.
choices.C: announcing each movement to the audience.
choices.D: turning his stopwatch on and off.

candidates.evidence: that he marked by opening and closing the lid
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 1 says Tudor marked the movements by opening and closing the lid.

C.rationale: The passage does not mention any announcement.

D.rationale: He started a stopwatch, but the movements were marked by the lid.

hints: Find how the movements were marked.
candidates.remember: Answer detail questions from the exact sentence.

candidates.stem: Based on the passage, Cage would most likely say that the audience members who talked and walked out during the third movement:

choices.A: ruined the performance by interrupting its silence.
choices.B: proved that the piece had failed as a joke.
choices.C: should have been asked to leave before it began.
choices.D: became part of the sounds the piece was framing.

candidates.evidence: during the third, the audience itself, talking and walking out
candidates.explanation: Cage lists the audience's own talking and walking out among the sounds the silence framed.

A.rationale: Cage held that the piece was never meant to be silent.

B.rationale: Cage insisted the piece was not a joke.

C.rationale: Nothing in the passage supports this.

hints: What sounds did Cage say the piece framed?

strategy.explanation: Apply Cage's view to the audience's noise.

candidates.remember: Apply a stated view to a specific case.

candidates.stem: The main function of the third paragraph is to:

choices.A: describe how anechoic chambers are built and used.
choices.B: recount an experience that shaped Cage's view of silence.
choices.C: show that the audience in 1952 misunderstood the piece.

candidates.evidence: Cage had come to this view partly through an experience not long before
candidates.explanation: The paragraph recounts Cage's visit to the anechoic chamber and the conclusion he drew about silence, which underlies the piece.

A.rationale: The chamber is described only as the setting for Cage's experience.

C.rationale: The paragraph is about Cage's own experience, not the audience.

D.rationale: No critic appears in the third paragraph.

hints: What does the first sentence of paragraph 3 announce?
candidates.remember: Opening sentences often state a paragraph's purpose.

candidates.stem: According to the passage, the two sounds Cage heard in the anechoic chamber came from:
candidates.evidence: these were his own nervous system and his own blood in circulation
candidates.explanation: The engineer told Cage the sounds were his own nervous system and blood circulation.

A.rationale: The engineer identified the sounds as Cage's nervous system and blood.

B.rationale: The chamber was built to block outside sound.

D.rationale: The engineer explained the sounds; he did not make them.

candidates.remember: Answer detail questions from the exact sentence.

candidates.stem: The statement that "true silence does not exist for a living listener" (paragraph 3) most nearly means that:

choices.A: a living person always hears some sound, if only their own body.
choices.B: a listener can learn to hear perfect silence with enough practice.
choices.C: anechoic chambers do not work as designed.
choices.D: people dislike silence and avoid it whenever possible.

candidates.evidence: there is only sound we attend to and sound we do not
candidates.explanation: Even in a room built to absorb all sound, Cage heard his own body, so a living listener can never experience complete silence.

B.rationale: The statement says silence does not exist for a living listener at all.

C.rationale: The chamber worked; the sounds came from Cage himself.

D.rationale: The statement concerns hearing, not preference.

hints: What did the chamber experience show Cage?

strategy.explanation: Connect the statement to the chamber episode.

candidates.remember: Interpret a statement using the example that leads to it.

author_checklist.hardness: abstract claim tied to a specific example

candidates.stem: The two critical views described in the fourth paragraph differ mainly in whether 4′33″:

choices.A: was performed by David Tudor or by Cage.
choices.C: should be performed in a concert hall or outdoors.
choices.D: is a genuine musical work or mainly an idea.

candidates.evidence: For some, 4′33″ is a philosophical statement more than a musical work
candidates.explanation: One view treats it as a philosophical statement that loses force once understood; the other treats it as a genuine composition that changes with each performance.

A.rationale: Both views concern the piece's nature, not its performer.

B.rationale: The passage says it has three; the critics do not dispute this.

C.rationale: The critics do not discuss where it should be performed.

hints: What do the two groups of critics disagree about?

strategy.explanation: Contrast the two "For some" and "For others" sentences.

candidates.remember: Identify the precise point on which two views differ.

candidates.stem: In the final paragraph, the author suggests that both critical views:

choices.A: are wrong because 4′33″ is clearly a joke.
choices.B: miss how the piece changes the way people listen.
choices.C: are correct and cannot be reconciled.
choices.D: depend too heavily on the details of the 1952 performance.

candidates.evidence: Both views, perhaps, miss the piece's quietest achievement
candidates.explanation: The author says both views may miss the piece's achievement: changing how listeners attend to everyday sound.

A.rationale: The author treats the piece seriously.

C.rationale: The author says both may miss the piece's achievement.

D.rationale: The author does not criticize their reliance on that performance.

hints: What does the author say both views miss?

strategy.explanation: Paraphrase the first sentence of the last paragraph.

candidates.remember: An author can step back from a debate to make a different point.

author_checklist.hardness: author's position relative to two others

candidates.stem: As it is used in paragraph 2, the word frame most nearly means:
candidates.evidence: The performer's silence was meant to frame these sounds
candidates.explanation: The silence sets off ordinary sounds so listeners notice them, the way a frame sets off a picture.

B.rationale: This literal sense does not fit sounds.

C.rationale: "Frame" in the sense of framing someone does not fit.

D.rationale: The silence does not put the sounds into words.

hints: What does the silence do to the sounds?

strategy.explanation: Substitute each choice into the sentence.

candidates.remember: Choose the meaning that fits the context.

candidates.stem: Based on the passage, a researcher who tested the students in paragraph 2 only five minutes after studying would most likely have mistakenly concluded that:

choices.A: rereading a passage produces better memory than practicing recall.
choices.B: practicing recall produces better memory than rereading after a week.
choices.C: students forget most of what they learn within the first day.
choices.D: students who practice recall feel more confident about remembering.

candidates.evidence: Five minutes later, the students who had reread the passage remembered slightly more
candidates.explanation: At five minutes, rereaders did slightly better, so a researcher who stopped there would wrongly conclude that rereading is the better method.

B.rationale: A five-minute test could not reveal results after a week.

C.rationale: The passage attributes this to Ebbinghaus, not to the five-minute test.

D.rationale: The rereaders were the more confident group.

hints: What did the five-minute test show?

strategy.explanation: Compare the five-minute and one-week results.

candidates.remember: Results can reverse depending on when they are measured.

author_checklist.hardness: requires reasoning about what a partial test would show

revision_history.reason: both solvers: stem asked which "result" would mislead, but the choices are conclusions
revision_history.change: stem reworded to ask what the researcher would mistakenly conclude; choices phrased as conclusions
